why_jerusalem.eyebrow: Why learn with a rabbi in Israel
why_jerusalem.headline: Some things are best learned at the source.
paragraphs: For generations, Jewish children have learned to read the Torah the same way: from a teacher who learned from a teacher, a chain that leads back to Jerusalem.

Our rabbis live and teach in Israel. The Hebrew your child chants from the Torah is the Hebrew their rabbi hears at the market, at the bus stop, around the Shabbat table. Many of the places named in the Torah are part of their everyday life.

And something shifts when a child realizes who is on the other side of the screen. The lesson stops being homework. It becomes a relationship with a real person in a real place, and a thread to Israel your child carries long after the big day.

how_it_works.headline: From first call to the big day, in four steps.
how_it_works.intro: No apps to learn and no travel. Just a laptop, a quiet corner and a rabbi who is glad to see your child.

steps.title: Book a free consultation
steps.text: A relaxed video call. Tell us about your child, your date, your community's customs and what matters most to your family.

steps.title: Meet your rabbi
steps.text: We match you with an Israeli rabbi who speaks your language and suits your child's personality, goals and tradition.

steps.title: Learn live, one-on-one
steps.text: Private Zoom lessons at times that work for your family, always shown in your local time. Every lesson is recorded for practice in between.

steps.title: Arrive ready

curriculum.headline: Everything for the big day, and the meaning behind it.
curriculum.intro: Every plan is built around your child's date, Torah portion and community. Here is what it can include.

cards.title: Reading from the Torah
cards.text: Learning to leyn their Torah portion (parasha) with the trope (ta'amim), the cantillation marks that give every word its melody.

cards.title: The aliyah blessings
cards.text: The blessings before and after the Torah reading, learned until they are said with ease and understood, not just memorized.

cards.title: Haftarah and maftir
cards.text: Chanting the Haftarah with its own melody, and preparing the maftir reading if your synagogue includes it.

cards.title: Tefillin
cards.text: How to put on tefillin, the blessings, and what they mean, so the first time is a proud moment, not a nervous one.

cards.title: Writing the speech (drasha)
cards.text: Your rabbi helps your child find their own message in the portion and turn it into a speech they are proud to give.

cards.title: Torah learning, beyond the day
cards.text: The stories, values and questions of the weekly portion, for children and adults who simply want to keep learning.

rabbis.headline: Israeli rabbis. Patient teachers. Fluent in your language.
rabbis.intro: Every rabbi on our team lives in Israel and teaches in English or French. They are chosen for something you cannot put on a résumé: the patience to meet a child exactly where they are, and the warmth to make them want to come back next week.

faq.headline: Questions parents ask us.

items.question: We live far from Israel. How do lesson times work across time zones?
items.answer: You book in your own time, not Israel time. Every lesson appears in your local time zone, in the parent portal and in every reminder, so there's no calculating. During the consultation we look at your child's week (school, activities, Shabbat) and find regular slots that actually fit.

items.question: What language are the lessons in? Does my child need to speak Hebrew?
items.answer: Your rabbi teaches in English (or French, if you prefer). The Torah, the blessings and the Haftarah are read in Hebrew, of course, but everything is explained in your language. Your child does not need to speak Hebrew: we start from wherever they are today.

items.question: We're Sephardi (or Ashkenazi). Will our child learn our tradition?
items.answer: Yes. The melodies of the Torah reading and the Haftarah, the pronunciation and the wording of the blessings vary between communities. Tell us your tradition during the consultation and we'll match you with a rabbi who can teach it the way your family and community do it.

items.question: Our synagogue has its own customs. Can you prepare our child for exactly what they'll do on the day?
items.answer: That's exactly how we work. Share what your synagogue expects: how much of the portion your child will read, whether there's a maftir and Haftarah, which blessings, any recordings from your cantor or rabbi. Your rabbi prepares your child for that, and nothing they won't need.

items.question: My child has ADHD (or dyslexia) and finds school hard. Will this work for them?
items.answer: Very often, one-on-one learning is exactly what these children need. Your rabbi adapts the pace, keeps lessons focused and varied, breaks the material into small steps and celebrates real progress. Recordings let your child practice in short bursts at home. Tell us about your child at the consultation, so we can choose the right rabbi and approach together.

items.question: Is this only for children? I'm an adult and never had a Bar or Bat Mitzvah.
items.answer: Not at all. Adults are very welcome: preparing an adult Bar or Bat Mitzvah, learning to read from the Torah for the first time, or simply studying Torah with a rabbi in Israel. It's the same private, one-on-one format, at your own pace.

items.question: How many lessons will my child need, and when should we start?
items.answer: It depends on your child's starting point, how much they'll read and how far away the date is. After the free consultation, your rabbi proposes a personal plan, so you'll know what's ahead before you pay. In general, starting earlier means a calmer pace, but if your date is close, talk to us: we'll tell you honestly what's realistic.

items.question: We're not religious. Is that a problem?
items.answer: Not at all, and you'll never be judged. Many families who aren't observant still want their child to feel connected to their Judaism, in a way that's meaningful for them. Your rabbi meets your family where you are, with respect and warmth.

items.question: How do you choose the rabbi for our child?
items.answer: We look at your language, your tradition and synagogue customs, your child's personality and needs, your goals and the times that work for you. Then we suggest the rabbi we believe is the best fit. If something doesn't feel right, tell us and we'll talk it through together.
